titleEn: Laws of Hammurabi — §278–282: the sale of slaves (xxxix 58 – xxxix 102)
part: Laws §278–282 · the sale of slaves (Col. xxxix 58 – xxxix 102)
about: The last five of the numbered laws. They deal with the sale of slaves, and with the slave who denies his master. A slave who falls sick with bennu within a month of the sale is handed back, and the buyer takes back his silver (§278); if a claim comes against a bought slave, the seller answers it (§279); a man who buys a slave abroad and brings him home may lose him to his old owner, who recognises him: if the slave is a native of Babylonia he is set free without payment (§280), and if he is a native of another country the buyer declares his price before the god and the owner pays that to the merchant and takes him back (§281). The final law is the slave who says to his master “You are not my master”: the master proves him his slave and cuts off his ear (§282). After this the numbered laws are over: the next column (xl) begins the epilogue, where Hammurabi turns from the cases to the people who will read and keep them. Col. xxxix is followed to line 102, its last; Harper’s line numerals agree with his headings. A few words are uncertain and the notes say so: bennu (a sickness), utēddi, ipaq and the idiom baqrī irtaši.

sentences.i: If a man has bought a male or a female slave,
sentences.n: This is the code’s last block of numbered laws (§278–282): the sale of slaves. They open with the usual šumma awīlum “if a man” and a verb in the perfect or preterite. wardam amtam “a male slave, a female slave” is written with two Sumerograms (words written in Sumerian signs): ARAD, one sign, and GEME₂, two signs, SAL and KUR drawn close together. On the stone both stand bare, without the ending -am that Harper’s normalised spelling wardam, amtam suggests; I write the signs the plate shows and supply the accusative from the grammar (they are the object of the verb). išāmma is išām, the 3rd-person singular of šâmum “to buy” (not the homonym “to fix destinies” of the prologue), plus -ma “and”. išām can be a present or a preterite; I take it, like īgur “has hired” earlier, as a preterite in the condition: “has bought”. The clause runs on into the next unit.

sentences.l: his-month not has-been-full-and, the-bennu-sickness on-him has-fallen, to his-seller he-shall-give-back-and,
sentences.i: and his month is not yet full and the bennu-sickness has fallen on him, he shall give him back to his seller, and
sentences.n: A sale with a one-month limit: if a sickness strikes the slave before the month is out, he goes back to the seller and the buyer gets his silver back. ITI-šu is ITI “month” (a Sumerogram, 𒌗) plus šu “his”; Harper prints arḫišu, but as the subject of the clause I expect the nominative, warḫušu “his month”. lā imlāma is imlâ, the preterite of malûm “to be full”, with lā “not” and -ma “and”: “his month has not become full”. bi-en-ni is the name of a sickness, bennu; Harper’s glossary says only “a kind of fever”, and I do not know what the illness was, so I leave it as the name. The ending -i is not the nominative and I cannot explain it. e-li-šu elīšu “upon him”; imtaqut (written im-ta-ku-ut, with the KU sign for qu) is the perfect of maqātum “to fall” (the verb of the “fall” of a house in earlier laws): “has fallen on him”. ana nādinānišu “to his seller” is one word, na-di-na-ni-šu, split across the line-end: na-di-na- at the end of line 62 and -ni-šu at the start of 63. utārma is utâr, the present of târum in the D-stem (turrum “to give back”) plus -ma: “he shall give back, and”. The sense of the whole sentence is clear; the word for the illness is the only unknown.

sentences.i: the buyer shall take back the silver he paid.
sentences.n: The apodosis (the “then” part). ša-a-a-ma-nu-um is the buyer, šayyāmānum (the opposite of nādinānum “seller”, as in §9). kaspam išqulu is “the silver he weighed out”, a relative clause with no ša: išqulu is išqul, the preterite of šaqālum “to weigh out” (silver is paid by weight, so “to pay”), with the subjunctive ending -u that marks a verb inside a relative clause. KÙ.BABBAR is the Sumerogram for kaspum “silver” (as in the earlier laws; two signs, KÙ and BABBAR); the plate has no -am after it. The qu₂ of iš-qu₂-lu is the sign KU read qu₂, as in earlier parts. i-li-qi₂ is ileqqi, the present of leqûm “to take”, written with the sign KI read qi₂: “he shall take”. On the plate, line 66 looks to me like one sign-group more than the three syllables i, li, qi₂ account for, and I cannot match every wedge; I follow Harper’s reading.

sentences.l: If a-man a-male-slave a-female-slave has-bought-and claims he-has-acquired,
sentences.i: If a man has bought a male or a female slave and claims have arisen against him (?),
sentences.n: The same opening as §278 (see there for ARAD and GEME₂). ba-aq-ri is the plural of a word for “claim”, which I read baqrī: Harper’s glossary lists it as bakru “claim”, from the verb baqārum “to make a claim”, met in §178–194. The sign is AK (Harper writes ag here and ak in his glossary), which I read aq, as in ipaq below, because the word has q in this edition. The plural ending -ī is the oblique case, as the object of the verb. ir-ta-ši is irtaši, the perfect of rašûm “to acquire, to get”, and is written on its own half-row under the line (Harper marks it {b}); literally “he has acquired claims”. I read that as an idiom, “claims have arisen against him”; the sense (a claim brought against the slave, or through him against the buyer) is clear from the next unit, but I am not sure of the idiom, nor of whom “he” is, so the English carries (?).

sentences.i: his seller shall answer the claims.
sentences.n: na-di-na-an-šu is nādinānšu, “his seller” (nādinānum “seller”, with -šu “his”; the n before the š stays, as the writing na-di-na-an-šu shows, the AN sign being the one that carries it). ba-aq-ri as in the unit above (baqrī, “claims”). i-ip-pa-al is ippal, the present of apālum “to answer, to satisfy”: the seller must meet the claims, not the buyer. The present here is the code’s ordinary “shall”.

sentences.l: If a-man in-the-land-of hostility a-male-slave a-female-slave of a-man has-bought,
sentences.i: If a man has bought, in a hostile country, a male or a female slave belonging to a man,
sentences.n: A long law with a double condition, written in five units. nukurtim is nukurtum “enmity, hostility” (Harper’s glossary: “enmity”) in the genitive; māt nukurtim “the land of hostility” is a foreign, enemy country. ma-at is māt, the form of mātum “land” that stands before a following noun in the genitive (the “construct state”: māt, “the land of”). wardam amtam ša awīlim “a male slave or female slave of a man”: ARAD and GEME₂ as in §278, and ša “of”; whose slave is not said. iš-ta-am is ištām, the perfect of šâmum “to buy” (the same verb as išām in §278, here in its perfect: “has bought”).

sentences.i: when he has come into the middle of the land,
sentences.n: inūma “when”. i-na li-ib-bu KALAM is ina libbu mātim “in the middle of the land”, that is, inside Babylonia itself (as opposed to the hostile country). Harper prints libbu (his glossary lists it so), not the libbi one expects after ina; I keep his form and say libbu. mātim is the Sumerogram KALAM “land”, which Harper normalises to mâtim; it is written with the single sign, no ending (as in the prologue). it-ta-al-kam-ma is ittalkamma: ittalkam, the perfect of alākum “to go” with the ventive -am (“to here”, so “has come”), plus -ma “and”. The verb that completes this clause is in the next unit.

sentences.l: the-owner of-the-male-slave or of-the-female-slave, either his-male-slave or his-female-slave, has-identified (?),
sentences.i: and the owner of the male or the female slave has identified (?) his male slave or his female slave,
sentences.n: bēl wardim ulu amtim “the owner of the male slave or the female slave” (bēl, written be-el, “owner”; ARAD and GEME₂ in the genitive, no ending written). The word for “or” is the conjunction ù “and” followed by lu “or”, written as two signs, as in §258–277 (the plate has the sign Ù, not ulu). lū warassu u lū amassu “whether his male slave or his female slave”: lū … u lū … “either … or”. ARAD-zu and GEME₂-zu are the two Sumerograms with the possessive -šu (ZU), pronounced warassu and amassu (the d of wardum and the t of amtum are assimilated to the š of -šu), as in the earlier laws. The verb is u-te-id-di, which I read utēddi: the D-stem perfect (so Harper’s glossary) of edûm “to know”, “to identify, to recognise”, the verb of uwaddīma in §185–194 (an uncertain reading there too). The form and the sense are uncertain; “has identified” suits a man who finds his own slave again.

sentences.l: If the-male-slave and the-female-slave they sons-of the-land,
sentences.i: If the male slave and the female slave are natives of the country,
sentences.n: A new condition: the slaves are natives. šunu “they” (šu-nu), the pronoun that makes a nominal sentence: “they (are) …”. mārū mātim, literally “sons of the land”, DUMU{meš} (DUMU, “son”, with the plural signs ME and EŠ, silent) and ma-tim, written with syllables here (the Sumerogram KALAM is used only in line 78); it means those born in the country. Harper normalises mârê; as a predicate I read the nominative plural mārū. In the plate, wardum and amtum are again the bare signs.

sentences.i: their release shall be set, without any silver.
sentences.n: The apodosis. ba-lum “without” (balum; Harper’s glossary lists it so). kaspi-ma is kaspima, the Sumerogram KÙ.BABBAR (see §278) plus -ma, which here stresses the “without”: “without silver (at all)”; Harper writes the word kaspi-ma, and I keep that. an-du-ra-ar-šu-nu is andurāršunu, “their release” (andurārum, here the freedom of a slave; a word known from §117 and §171), with -šunu “their”. iš-ša-ak-ka-an is iššakkan, the N-stem (passive) present of šakānum “to set”: “shall be set, shall be established”, the same word as in §117. The word order is that of earlier laws.

sentences.i: If they are natives of another country,
sentences.n: The second case. mārū mātim šanītim: “sons of another land”, that is, natives of a foreign country; DUMU{meš}, ma-tim and ša-ni-tim (šanītim, the feminine genitive of šanûm “another”, agreeing with mātim). This line stands alone: the plate has it on two half-rows. In the printed transliteration of §281 the carons are very faint; the signs are those of the plate (šum-ma, ša-ni-tim). The clause has no verb; “they are” has to be supplied, as in the unit above. Harper normalises mârê; the predicate nominative is mārū.

sentences.l: the-buyer before the-god the-silver (that) he-weighed-out shall-declare-and,
sentences.i: the buyer shall declare, before the god, the silver he paid, and
sentences.n: ša-a-a-ma-nu-ma is šayyāmānum “the buyer” with -ma, which here marks the clause that follows the condition (“as for the buyer: …”). ina maḫar ilim is “before the god”, as in §266 (a formal declaration in the god’s presence; the law does not say “oath” here): “before” is ma-ḫar and the god is written i-lim syllabically, not with the divine sign AN. kaspam išqulu “the silver he weighed out” (see §278). i-qa₂-ab-bi-ma is iqabbi, the present of qabûm “to say” (as in iqtabi, §282), with -ma: “he shall say, he shall declare”. Harper prints the GA sign as ga; it is read qa₂ here, as in earlier parts.

sentences.l: the-owner of-the-male-slave or of-the-female-slave the-silver (that) he-weighed-out to the-merchant shall-give-and,
sentences.i: the owner of the male or the female slave shall give the silver that was paid to the merchant, and
sentences.n: bēl wardim ù lū amtim as in §280. kaspam išqulu again, “the silver he weighed out”: the silver the buyer paid. ana tamkārim “to the merchant”: tamkārum, written DAM.GÀR, two Sumerograms (DAM and GÀR, no ending). Who the merchant is is not said; I take him to be the man from whom the buyer bought the slave abroad (my inference, not the text’s): the owner pays him back what the buyer paid. i-na-ad-di-in-ma is inaddin, the present of nadānum “to give”, with -ma: “he shall give, and”.

sentences.i: he shall take back (?) his male slave or his female slave.
sentences.n: lū warassu lū amassu “either his male slave or his female slave” (see §280 for ARAD-zu and GEME₂-zu). i-pa-aq is the verb. Harper’s glossary lists it as ipaq, from a verb he writes paku, “to receive into one’s care, to be entrusted with”; the last sign is AK read aq. I do not know the word certainly. The sense “takes back, takes into his own care” fits the situation, the owner who has paid the merchant recovering his slave, but this is UNCERTAIN and I say so with the (?).

sentences.l: If a-male-slave to his-master “not my-master you” has-said,
sentences.i: If a slave has said to his master, “You are not my master,”
sentences.n: The last law of the code: a slave who disowns his master. The condition is šumma wardum ana bēlišu … iqtabi “if a slave has said to his master …”: iq-ta-bi is iqtabi, the perfect of qabûm “to say”, with the sign IG read iq; the words said are quoted without any quotation word, as in §192 (“You are not my father”). ul bēlī atta is “not my master you (are)”: bēlī, spelled be-li, is bēlum with the “my” ending -ī; atta “you (m.)” is at-ta; ul “not” is u-ul. The words are a denial of the owner’s claim on him. wardum is ARAD, bare.

sentences.l: as his-male-slave he-shall-convict-him-and his-master his-ear he-shall-cut-off.
sentences.i: his master shall prove him to be his slave and cut off his ear.
sentences.n: The penalty, in two clauses with the same subject, the master. kīma warassu is “as his slave” (ARAD-zu, as in §280; kīma “like, as”). u-ka-an-šu-ma is ukān-šu-ma: ukān, the present of kânum in the D-stem (kunnum “to prove, to convict”, as in the earlier laws), with -šu “him” and -ma “and”: “he shall convict him as his slave”, that is, prove before the court that the man is his slave. bēlšu “his master”, and then uznašu inakkis: uznum “ear” (written u-zu-un-šu, with Harper’s normalisation uznašu) and inakkis, the present of nakāsum “to cut off” (the verb of the tongue in §192 and the breast in §194): “he shall cut off his ear”. The penalty is literally cutting off the ear. With this the numbered laws end; the epilogue begins just below, in column XL, on the same plate.
